parts.partTitle: Class Blueprints & Heap vs Metaspace Memory

beats.headline: Loose arrays and floating variables will wreck your app.
beats.subline: Classes bundle state and behavior into a single cohesive unit.
beats.narration: Tracking financial balances across loose arrays quickly creates severe data sync bugs. Object-oriented programming fixes this by wrapping state and behavior inside a single compiled blueprint called a class.

beats.title: Metaspace vs Heap Memory
beats.subtitle: Method bytecode is shared while fields belong to instances

nodes.label: Metaspace
nodes.detail: Stores class metadata & shared method bytecode

beats.narration: Class metadata and compiled bytecode reside once inside Metaspace. When you allocate objects on the Heap, each instance gets its own field values while sharing that exact same bytecode in Metaspace.

beats.title: Encapsulating State in Java

steps.explanation: Encapsulates state so callers cannot write balance directly.
Enforces business rules before mutating balance.

beats.narration: In this class, private fields enforce encapsulation so external code cannot corrupt account balance. Every mutation must pass through public methods that validate business logic.

beats.title: Procedural Data vs Encapsulated Class

top.label: Procedural Arrays

beats.narration: Procedural arrays decouple state from logic, causing hard-to-track bugs. Java classes protect fields with validated methods, guaranteeing your invariants remain enforced across your entire app.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Classes are blueprints loaded into Metaspace
Objects are distinct memory allocations on the Heap
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): What happens during object instantiation with new →
beats.narration: That is the core class model. Next in Part 2, we trace the exact four-step memory pipeline the JVM executes every time you call new.

beats.headline: A constructor with a return type is not a constructor.
beats.subline: Adding void turns it into a standard method that never initializes objects.
beats.narration: Adding void to a constructor signature turns it into a regular method. The compiler won't complain, but calling new will completely bypass your initialization logic.

beats.title: The 4-Step Object Initialization Pipeline
beats.subtitle: What the JVM executes during new BankAccount()

nodes.label: 1. Heap Memory
nodes.detail: Reserves Heap space for object header and fields

nodes.label: 2. Zero Init
nodes.detail: Sets fields to default 0, 0.0, false, or null

nodes.label: 4. Return Reference
nodes.detail: Assigns Heap reference address to variable

beats.narration: When calling new, the JVM reserves Heap memory, zero-initializes fields to defaults, executes constructor init bytecode, and finally returns the reference address to your variable.

beats.title: Shadowing & Constructor Chaining

steps.explanation: Delegates to master constructor; must be the first statement.
Resolves parameter shadowing against instance fields.

beats.narration: Use this to resolve parameter shadowing when argument names match class fields. You can also chain constructors using this with arguments, which must be the very first statement.

beats.title: Inspecting Synthesized Constructors
beats.caption: javap reveals javac bytecode generation

lines.text: # Disassemble compiled bytecode for Counter class

beats.narration: Disassembling a class file reveals compiler internals. Omitting constructors causes javac to automatically generate a default no-argument constructor calling Object's init method under the hood.

beats.title: Constructor Mechanics Mastered
takeaways: Constructors have no return type—not even void
JVM zero-initializes fields before constructor code runs
Explicit constructors suppress compiler default no-arg generation

parts.partTitle: The this Keyword Bytecode & Static vs Instance Methods

beats.headline: Instance methods receive a hidden argument you never wrote.
beats.subline: Slot 0 in local variable tables automatically holds the this reference.
beats.narration: Instance methods don't magically know which object called them. At the bytecode level, the JVM silently passes the target object reference as hidden parameter zero.

beats.title: Disassembling Method Calls

steps.explanation: Reads hidden this reference passed implicitly into local variable slot 0.

beats.narration: Inspecting compiled bytecode shows aload_0 pushing this from local variable slot zero onto the operand stack. Static methods belong to the class itself, so they lack slot zero completely.

beats.title: Instance Methods vs Static Utilities

top.label: Instance Method

bottom.label: Static Method
points: No instance target; referencing this fails

beats.narration: Use static methods for stateless pure functions that rely only on parameters. Use instance methods when logic depends on fields belonging to a specific object instance.

beats.title: Fluent Builder Pattern with return this

steps.explanation: Returns current instance reference to enable method chaining.

beats.narration: Returning this from instance methods enables fluent method chaining. Callers can trigger consecutive configuration calls on a single target instance in a clean readable chain.

beats.title: Method Semantics Locked In
takeaways: aload_0 passes hidden this reference to instance methods
Static methods belong to classes and have no this reference
Returning this enables fluent method chaining

parts.partTitle: Object References, Memory Aliasing & NPE Diagnostics

beats.headline: Copying an object variable never copies the object.
beats.subline: Variables hold remote memory addresses, not the underlying data.
beats.narration: Assigning one object variable to another never copies data on the Heap. It only copies the reference address, creating two pointers to the exact same object.

beats.title: Stack References & Heap Objects
beats.subtitle: Two variables aliasing a single Heap instance
beats.narration: Stack variables hold reference addresses pointing to Heap locations. When two variables share an address, modifying object state through one reference instantly updates what the other sees.

beats.title: Reference Equality vs Value Equality

top.label: == Operator

bottom.label: .equals() Method
points: Standard for strings and domain objects

beats.narration: Using double equals compares whether two reference variables point to the identical memory address. To compare actual field values across separate objects, always call the equals method instead.

beats.title: Helpful NullPointerExceptions (Java 14+)
beats.caption: Precise diagnostic message pinpoints null references

lines.text: # Executing method call on a null variable

beats.narration: Invoking methods on null references throws a NullPointerException. Modern Java prints exact diagnostic details in the stack trace, identifying the precise variable that evaluated to null.
